hints: Look carefully at Fig. 4.1 - which ventricle has the much thicker grey band of cardiac muscle, and where does each ventricle pump blood to?
walkthrough:
Spot the structural difference**
You can see in Fig. 4.1 that the grey cardiac muscle around the left ventricle is much thicker than around the right ventricle. Thicker muscle means more muscle fibres to contract, so it can squeeze more forcefully.

Match each ventricle to its circulation**
The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs in the pulmonary circulation. The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood to the rest of the body in the systemic circulation. That is the key functional difference.

Explain why pressure needs differ**
The systemic circuit is very long, goes to all tissues, and has high resistance, so blood must leave the left ventricle at high pressure to complete the circuit and return to the heart. The pulmonary circuit is very short, lungs are close to the heart, with lower resistance, so the right ventricle only needs to generate low pressure. That is why the left wall is thicker.

Final answer: Left ventricle wall is much thicker than right ventricle wall. Left ventricle pumps blood around systemic circulation to the whole body over a long distance against high resistance, so needs powerful contraction to generate high pressure. Right ventricle pumps blood only a short distance to the lungs in pulmonary circulation, so lower pressure is needed.

hints: A steep gradient needs high oxygen on the alveolus side and low oxygen on the blood side - how is the air side kept topped up with fresh oxygen?
How is the blood side kept low in oxygen, so oxygen keeps diffusing in and does not build up?
Apply the marking criteria to conclude your answer.
Apply the marking criteria to conclude your answer.
walkthrough:
Keep the alveolar side high**
Think of diffusion as flowing downhill from high to low. Breathing in, or ventilation, constantly replaces the air in the alveoli with fresh inhaled air rich in oxygen, while breathing out removes air that has lost oxygen. This keeps alveolar oxygen concentration high.

Keep the blood side low**
On the other side, the heart keeps pumping blood through the alveolar capillaries. Deoxygenated blood arriving is low in oxygen, and as soon as oxygen diffuses in it is removed in the flowing blood and also taken up by haemoglobin to form oxyhaemoglobin. This prevents oxygen building up in the plasma, so the blood stays low in free oxygen and the gradient stays steep.

Final answer: Ventilation / breathing movements continually bring in fresh air high in oxygen and remove air low in oxygen, maintaining high alveolar $O_2$. Continuous blood flow brings deoxygenated blood low in oxygen and removes oxygenated blood, and haemoglobin loads oxygen to form oxyhaemoglobin, keeping dissolved oxygen in blood low.

hints: Smoking irritates the lining of the trachea, bronchi and bronchioles - what would happen to the width of the airway lumen if muscle contracts or mucus builds up?
walkthrough:
From irritation to narrower tubes**
Chemicals in tobacco smoke irritate the airways. The smooth muscle in bronchi and bronchioles contracts, the lining becomes inflamed and swollen, and goblet cells secrete extra mucus. All of these narrow the lumen, increase resistance to airflow, and reduce the volume of air per breath reaching the alveoli.
Final answer: Smoke irritants cause contraction of smooth muscle / narrowing of airway lumen and / or inflammation and / or excess mucus blocking airways, so less air reaches alveoli.

hints: Tobacco smoke contains a gas that competes with oxygen for the same binding site on haemoglobin - recall which gas this is.
Think about how strongly and permanently this gas binds, and what that means for the number of haem groups left free to carry oxygen.
walkthrough:
Meet the competitor gas**
Tobacco smoke contains carbon monoxide. It diffuses across the alveoli just like oxygen and reaches red blood cells, where it competes for the $Fe^{2+}$ haem groups on haemoglobin.

Block the oxygen seats**
Carbon monoxide binds much more strongly than oxygen and almost irreversibly to form carboxyhaemoglobin. Once bound it does not easily release, so those haemoglobin molecules can no longer load and transport oxygen, reducing the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood.

Final answer: Carbon monoxide in smoke binds to haemoglobin, competing with oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin. Binding is strong / effectively irreversible, so fewer haem groups available to carry oxygen.
